summary:
TWIN (Terrestrial World Identification Network) is an interactive map that matches Moon and Mars sites to their closest analogues on Earth. Users explore a Moon globe and a Mars globe built from NASA LRO and Viking mosaics, pick a landing site or surface feature, and see Earth locations that resemble it. Twenty Earth sites are compared across eight traits: geology, terrain, temperature and light, water and ice, dust and wind, biology, caves and subsurface, and operations. A compare and rank tool lets users weight the traits for their own mission and ranks the sites, favouring those that were backed by a cited twin from a space agency or peer-reviewed sources. 

This addresses the challenge of finding Earth locations that are analogues for permanent Moon base sites and Mars. Before costly missions, crews, rovers and equipment must be trained and tested on Earth, but analogue knowledge is scattered across agencies and papers. TWIN puts it in one place, with sources on a References page, so planners can choose where to rehearse.
details:
What it does. TWIN is an interactive web map for finding where on Earth to rehearse for the Moon and Mars. Users explore a Moon globe and a Mars globe, select a landing site or surface feature, and see the Earth sites that most resemble it. Each of 20 Earth sites is marked yes or no on eight traits: geology and mineralogy; terrain and topography; temperature, light and extremes; water, ice and resources; dust, wind and erosion; biology and biosignatures; caves and subsurface; and operations (landing, mobility, crew, construction). A Compare & rank tool lets users weight each trait from 0 to 5 and scores every site by the weighted share of its ticked traits, plus a bonus for sites with a cited twin. Defaults differ by world: geology and terrain lead for the Moon, while geology, water, terrain and biology lead for Mars.

Data. The globes use NASA’s LRO LROC WAC and Viking MDIM 2.1 mosaics via USGS Astropedia. Feature and landing-site positions come from the IAU/USGS Gazetteer (21 features) and NASA NSSDCA (13 missions). A live sky layer uses NASA GSFC Moon phases, NASA GISS Mars24 and JPL planetary positions. Analog claims are backed by pages from CSA, ESA, ISRO, USGS and NASA, plus 55 peer-reviewed papers, all listed on a References page.

Benefits and impact. Analog knowledge is scattered across agencies and papers. TWIN puts it in one transparent place, so mission planners, educators and students can see why a site matches and which sources support it, and can choose where to train crews and test equipment before costly missions.

Creativity. Instead of a static list of analog sites, users judge for themselves by re-weighting what matters for their mission, in a map styled after the CFR Global Conflict Tracker.

Factors considered. We kept claims honest: the traits are ticks from our research sheet, not measurements, so we show no temperatures or elevations. Data sources are credited, and the References page lists them.

Tools and software. HTML5, CSS3 and plain JavaScript, with no framework and no build step. Libraries, all served from the site itself: globe.gl 2.46.2 (includes three.js) for the 3D globes, Leaflet 1.9.4 for the locator maps, and topojson-client 3.1.0 for the country borders (Natural Earth). The Live sky page embeds Stellarium Web, which loads only on click. Fonts: Inter and Libre Caslon Text (SIL Open Font License). Hosted on Cloudflare Pages, deployed from a GitHub repository.
